title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $\epsilon$-close Surrogates
claim: Our lifted approach achieves higher success rates than competing non-convex and relaxation baselines across problem sizes and observation settings.
layout: 2 side-by-side horizontal grouped bar charts, shared problem-size axis, 'no success' labels
description: Two side-by-side horizontal grouped bar charts compare success rates (x-axis, 0 to 1) across problem sizes n=4 through n=8 (y-axis). Panel (a), titled 'Problem Instance (24)', shows four methods: BM Factorization (light blue), GNMR (green), and Our Approach (Lifted) (gray). Panel (b), 'Independent Entries with p = 0.15', adds SDP Relaxation (orange) and Lin-RFM (purple). Small gray 'no success' labels mark methods that failed entirely. In (a), the gray bars for our approach are the longest at 0.4 to 0.6 and the baselines stay under 0.25. In (b), our approach reaches about 0.25 to 0.3, and Lin-RFM spikes to 0.8 at n=4. A legend sits in the top-right of each panel. The eye goes first to the long gray bars and the purple outlier.
caption: We use $\epsilon=5\times10^{-5}$, a learning rate of $2\times10^{-2}$, and an initialization scale of $\xi=10^{-4}$ for [ref]. SDP was not deployed for (a) since the solution is not unique in the relaxed regime. For (b), the variability of $\Omega$ necessitates running 10 distinct problem instances for each size $n$.
abstract: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $Îµ$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(Îµ)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.
